archetype.name: Gunslinger (veteran spot starter)
archetype.definition: An 11th-year backup with a big arm and a long history of holding the ball and pushing it downfield, which brings both splash plays and sacks and turnovers when the timing isn't there.

report.headline: Two spot starts, one disaster: Wentz is a stopgap, not a solution
report.take:
Wentz is a well-traveled veteran with a wide career range. In 2017 he posted a 0.246 EPA per play, third in the league. Since then he has bounced between average and below-average seasons. He now backs up Kyler Murray in a Minnesota offense that ranks 31st in EPA, and his 2026 is three appearances: he took over early in a Week 1 win over Green Bay, then started a 9-3 slog at Chicago in Week 2 and a 6-23 loss to Buffalo in Week 9. As a starter he has completed 42.2% of his passes for 4.98 yards an attempt, with no touchdowns, two interceptions and -0.491 EPA per dropback. That is what the Vikings get from him right now.

The season splits into two halves. The first two games were survivable: positive passing EPA both times, with a defense that ranks first in the league carrying the results. Buffalo was the collapse: 8 of 25, 81 yards, two interceptions, a lost fumble and -24.6 passing EPA with a -30.7 CPOE. He also played his most aggressively that day, throwing into tight windows on 32% of attempts and holding the ball 3.13 seconds. That single afternoon accounts for most of a season line that ranks 43rd of 49 in EPA per dropback and 48th in CPOE.

The numbers hide two things. First, his bad-throw rate of 12.5% is better than last season's 18.9%, even as his CPOE fell from +1.1 to -15.4. That gap points less to broken mechanics and more to target difficulty: aggressiveness is up to 20.31% from 14.8%, and the outside throws have been brutal, especially to the right (-0.394 EPA per play). Second, the middle of the field has worked, with +0.152 EPA and 65% completions, mostly on throws to his tight ends. The connection with Justin Jefferson has been close to neutral, and Jordan Addison's targets have been a drain.

Where it's heading depends on Murray's hamstring. The estimated return date is this Sunday. If Murray makes it, Wentz goes back to the bench. If he doesn't, expect a conservative, defense-first plan in which Wentz is asked to work the middle, avoid sacks and not lose the game. Last year's 7.2 yards per attempt suggests the true level is somewhat better than this sample. It is still the level of a backup.

strengths.title: Middle of the field works
strengths.body: Between the numbers he has been a functional passer, completing 65% for positive EPA. The rest of the field has been sharply negative. Hockenson and Josh Oliver are his two efficient targets, which fits a quarterback who reads better with a defined, short-to-intermediate inside window than when he's challenging the sideline. It's a 20-attempt split, but it lines up with where the Vikings' tight ends live, so it's the right foundation for any game plan with him.

strengths.title: Last year says he's better
strengths.body: In five games in this offense last season he completed 65.1% at 7.2 yards an attempt with a +1.1 CPOE and a 0.06 EPA per play. That's a serviceable backup, not the -15 CPOE passer of this sample. His bad-throw rate has actually improved. Some of the 2026 accuracy crater is one game and tougher throws rather than a lost skill, so some bounce-back toward that baseline is the reasonable expectation.

concerns.title: Accuracy has fallen off a cliff
concerns.body: A -15.41 CPOE ranks 48th of 49, and in his two starts it sits at -19.5. The Buffalo game drives much of it, but Weeks 1 and 2 were also well below expectation. The cause looks like shot selection more than mechanics: he's throwing into tight windows more often than last year, and the outside throws, especially to the right, have been disastrous. Some regression upward is likely. Still, a passer who misses this often on harder throws needs a plan that keeps him off the sideline.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He's rarely pressured, which says more about the line and protection than about him. When he is, two-thirds of those pressures become sacks, last among 42 qualifiers. This isn't new: his pressure-to-sack rate ranked 46th last year and has sat near the bottom in several seasons. It is a career-long cost of holding the ball looking for something big, and it won't go away. The 9.9% sack rate is the result.

concerns.title: Outside receivers aren't producing
concerns.body: Jefferson has drawn the most targets by far, but they've produced roughly neutral EPA. Addison and Myles Price have been clearly negative. With the game within one score, his dropbacks have lost about as much EPA as his whole season total. The competitive snaps are where it's going wrong, not garbage time.

trend.note: Passing EPA went from +5 in Week 1 relief to +0.5 at Chicago to -24.6 against Buffalo. The most recent and largest sample is the worst, though it is a single game after a long layoff from playing.

nextGame.headline: If he starts, a low-total road game against a top-five pass defense
nextGame.body:
Green Bay's defense ranks fifth against the pass and fifth in limiting explosive passes. It allows the seventh-fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks. That is a poor fit for a passer whose problems are on outside and downfield throws. There are cracks, though. WR1s have beaten their usual output against this defense (26th of 32), which is a chance for Jefferson. Linebacker Zaire Franklin, a 99%-snap player, is out, and Ty'Ron Hopper is questionable, which softens the middle of the field where Wentz has been most effective. Micah Parsons is out but hasn't played this season, so that changes nothing about the Packers' profile. Wentz shredded this team in Week 1, but in relief and at home.

The first question is whether he plays at all. Murray's hamstring carries an estimated return date of this Sunday. Wentz is listed as QB2, so a Murray return sends him to the bench. Jauan Jennings, a 67%-snap receiver, is out with a calf injury on the same timeline. If Jennings misses, more targets go to depth receivers like Price, who have been negative with Wentz. On the other side, Green Bay is missing tackle Travis Glover, guard Sean Rhyan and its top backs, Josh Jacobs and MarShawn Lloyd. Against Minnesota's league-best pass rush, that points to a grinding, low-scoring game. The 41.5 total already says as much, and it means modest passing volume for Wentz.

keyMatchups.title: Middle reads versus thinned linebackers
keyMatchups.body: Wentz's only positive area has been between the numbers. Green Bay loses its every-down linebacker there. The Packers have held top tight ends well under their averages, so this isn't a guaranteed win. Still, Hockenson and Oliver over the middle is the matchup the Vikings should lean on.

keyMatchups.title: Jefferson against a WR1-friendly defense
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay has let lead receivers outplay their usual numbers, even while ranking fifth in pass EPA overall. Wentz's targets to Jefferson have been roughly break-even so far. Turning that into real gains is the clearest path to a respectable day.

keyMatchups.title: Vikings pass rush sets the script
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota's defense leads the league in sack rate. It faces a Green Bay line missing two starters and a backfield missing its top backs. If the defense controls the game, the Vikings can stay run-leaning and hide their quarterback. That caps his volume but protects him from obvious passing downs.

nextGame.watch: Murray's hamstring status first. If Wentz starts, watch whether he gets the ball out on time or keeps turning pressure into sacks.

restOfSeason.body:
Wentz's role is week-to-week insurance. Murray's expected return points to Wentz going back to the bench soon, and starts after that would come only with another injury. When he does play, expect better than this sample but not much better. His CPOE should drift back toward last year's level, since the bad-throw rate is fine and one game drives much of the damage. The structural limits stay, though: a 31st-ranked offense, a pressure-to-sack habit he's carried for years, and a defense-first script that keeps volume low.

As a starter, a reasonable range is something like 150 to 200 passing yards and up to about one touchdown a game, with two to three sacks. The interception risk rises when he chases the sideline. The red-zone touchdowns and the late-game efficiency rest on handfuls of plays and shouldn't be counted on.
swingFactors: Murray's hamstring and whether Wentz starts at all
Whether the Jefferson connection turns positive
Avoiding sacks on the pressures he does face

confidence.note: 64 attempts, two starts and an uncertain role tied to Murray's return.
